aggregated_directions.explanation: It appears that this feature is picking up boilerplate “page‐metadata” text—the kinds of fixed, formulaic phrases and formatting used in online posts, blog entries, and forum pages. In other words, it strongly activates on tokens that signal posting details (dates, times, “posted on…”, “filed under…”), navigation instructions (e.g. “skip to the end,” “follow”), legal disclaimers, placeholders, and names inserted by the site. This suggests the feature represents a detector for structured, context‐framing metadata and interface elements rather than the “content” of a post.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature is picking up boilerplate “page‐metadata” text—the kinds of fixed, formulaic phrases and formatting used in online posts, blog entries, and forum pages. In other words, it strongly activates on tokens that signal posting details (dates, times, “posted on…”, “filed under…”), navigation instructions (e.g. “skip to the end,” “follow”), legal disclaimers, placeholders, and names inserted by the site. This suggests the feature represents a detector for structured, context‐framing metadata and interface elements rather than the “content” of a post.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginnings of words—their initial sub‐token fragments—that are key semantic markers setting up the sentence’s topic or function. In other words, the feature is detecting and flagging word‐initial morphemic units (the “stems” or prefixes of words like “Prom” in “Promote,” “Expl” in “Explore,” “Activ” in “Activation,” etc.) which tend to signal the action, description, or domain being discussed. This burst of activation on the word‐onset segments seems to serve as a trigger that helps the model align subsequent processing with the overall semantic frame or purpose of the passage, regardless of domain.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature is picking up boilerplate “page‐metadata” text—the kinds of fixed, formulaic phrases and formatting used in online posts, blog entries, and forum pages. In other words, it strongly activates on tokens that signal posting details (dates, times, “posted on…”, “filed under…”), navigation instructions (e.g. “skip to the end,” “follow”), legal disclaimers, placeholders, and names inserted by the site. This suggests the feature represents a detector for structured, context‐framing metadata and interface elements rather than the “content” of a post.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginnings of words—their initial sub‐token fragments—that are key semantic markers setting up the sentence’s topic or function. direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature is picking up boilerplate “page‐metadata” text—the kinds of fixed, formulaic phrases and formatting used in online posts, blog entries, and forum pages. This suggests the feature represents a detector for structured, context‐framing metadata and interface elements rather than the “content” of a post.

direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginnings of words—their initial sub‐token fragments—that are key semantic markers setting up the sentence’s topic or function. In other words, the feature is detecting and flagging word‐initial morphemic units (the “stems” or prefixes of words like “Prom” in “Promote,” “Expl” in “Explore,” “Activ” in “Activation,” etc.) which tend to signal the action, description, or domain being discussed. This burst of activation on the word‐onset segments seems to serve as a trigger that helps the model align subsequent processing with the overall semantic frame or purpose of the passage, regardless of domain.

In many examples a punctuation token (almost always a period) following numbers, abbreviations or proper noun segments—and often coming at the end of a title, date, or identifier—triggers high activation. direction_summaries.explanation: It appears that this feature “lights up” on the beginnings of words—their initial sub‐token fragments—that are key semantic markers setting up the sentence’s topic or function. In other words, the feature is detecting and flagging word‐initial morphemic units (the “stems” or prefixes of words like “Prom” in “Promote,” “Expl” in “Explore,” “Activ” in “Activation,” etc.) which tend to signal the action, description, or domain being discussed. This burst of activation on the word‐onset segments seems to serve as a trigger that helps the model align subsequent processing with the overall semantic frame or purpose of the passage, regardless of domain.
